decision.explanation: With x fixed at -2, the tangent slope is dz/dy=f_y(-2,2)=4(2)-4-2=2. Through P, the tangent satisfies z-1=2(y-2), hence x=-2 and z=2y-3.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,2,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}(y-2) \\ z-1 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Given that the point $P(-2,2,1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}={x}^{2}y+2x-y$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(-2,2,1)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(-2,2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,2) & =(-2)^{2}(2)+2(-2)-(2) \\  & =8-4-2 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(-2,2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(-2,2)}(y-2) \\ z-1 & =2(y-2) \\ z & =2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,2,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=2y-3\end{aligned}
$$

after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=-1.$ Given that the point $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=\frac{x(y-x)}{2x(y+1)}$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=-1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(-1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,0) & =\frac{(-1)(0-(-1))}{2(-1)(0+1)} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,0) & ={f}_{y}(-1,0)(y-0) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-1,0,\frac{1}{2})$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(-1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-1,0) & =\frac{(-1)(0-(-1))}{2(-1)(0+1)} \\  & =\frac{-1}{-2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-1,0) & ={f}_{y}(-1,0)(y-0) \\ z-\frac{1}{2} & =\frac{1}{2}y \\ z & =\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-1 \\ z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

- For the plane $x=-1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=\frac{1}{2}y+\frac{1}{2}$ (or $y-2z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,-2⟩.$

decision.explanation: With y=-2 fixed, the tangent slope is dz/dx=f_x(4,-2)=-2√4=-4. Through P, z-5=-4(x-4), giving z=-4x+21 together with y=-2.

after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(4,-2,5)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(4,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)} & =(-2)\sqrt{4} \\  & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(4,-2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}(x-4) \\ z-5 & =-4(x-4) \\ z & =-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,-2,5)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Given that the point $P(4,-2,5)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=y\sqrt{x}$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $y=-2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(4,-2,5)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂x}$ at $(4,-2):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)} & =(-2)\sqrt{4} \\  & =-2(2) \\  & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(4,-2)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂x}{|}_{(4,-2)}(x-4) \\ z-5 & =-4(x-4) \\ z & =-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(4,-2,5)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=-2 \\ z=-4x+21\end{aligned}
$$

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=2. Given that the point P(2,π4,0) lies on C, and that fy=4sin⁡(xy), find the equations of the tangent line to C at P.

a

b

decision.explanation: With x=2 fixed, the tangent slope is f_y(2,π/4)=4sin(π/2)=4. Through P, z-0=4(y-π/4), so the tangent line is x=2, z=4y-π.

after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=2.$ Given that the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=4\operatorname{sin}⁡(xy)$, find the equations of the tangent line to $C$ at $P.$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface $z=f(x,y)$ with the plane $x=2.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve at the point $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ will be given by the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}.$

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative $\frac{∂z}{∂y}$ at $(2,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(2,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =4\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4}) \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}) \\  & =4\cdot 1 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-z{|}_{(2,\pi /4)} & =\frac{∂z}{∂y}{|}_{(2,\pi /4)}(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z-0 & =4(y-\frac{\pi }{4}) \\ z & =4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(2,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes, as follows:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=2 \\ z=4y-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
after.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$

The curve C is the intersection of a surface S, defined by z=f(x,y), with the plane x=1. Given that the point P(1,0,−1) lies on C, and that fy=xexy−2cos⁡y, which of the following gives a tangent vector to C at P?

a
−j+2k
b
−j+k
c
j+k
d
2j−3k
e
−2j+k
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The curve C is the intersection of the surface with the plane x=1. Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve C at the point P will be given by the partial derivative fy(1,0).

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative fy(x,y) at (1,0):

fy(1,0)=1⋅e1⋅0−2cos⁡0=1⋅1−2⋅1=−1

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

z−f(1,0)=fy(1,0)(y−0)z−(−1)=(−1)yz=−y−1

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve C at P(1,0,−1) can be given as the intersection of two planes: {x=1z=−y−1

Next, notice that:

  • For the plane x=1, a normal vector to the plane is n1=⟨1,0,0⟩.

  • For the plane z=−y−1 (or y+z+1=0), a normal vector to the plane is n2=⟨0,1,1⟩.

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

n1×n2=⟨1,0,0⟩×⟨0,1,1⟩=ijk100011=−j+k

Therefore, a tangent vector to C at P is −j+k.

content.problem: The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $x=1.$ Given that the point $P(1,0,-1)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{y}=x{e}^{xy}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$
content.worked_solution:
The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $x=1.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(1,0).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{y}(x,y)$ at $(1,0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(1,0) & =1\cdot {e}^{1\cdot 0}-2\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =1\cdot 1-2\cdot 1 \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,0) & ={f}_{y}(1,0)(y-0) \\ z-(-1) & =(-1)y \\ z & =-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,0,-1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=1 \\ z=-y-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $x=1,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-1$ (or $y+z+1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, a tangent vector to $C$ at $P$ is $-j+k.$
